notes: Rule edit. Derivability unlikely, not very_unlikely: the style also follows from a superclass rule stated more often than this one (Knight Bachelor is the basic rank of a knighted man, and Wikipedia's own article says 'A man who is knighted is formally addressed as "Sir"'), the same subclass route as people-replace-0007 (life peer, peer, House of Lords). The rule itself is stated too ('Knights Bachelor may prefix "Sir"'), so it is rated stored. R1: the rule is scoped to British laymen. Honorary (foreign) knights are not entitled to 'Sir', and clergy who are knighted are by tradition not dubbed and do not use 'Sir'; both fall outside the class. A Knight Bachelor who is later made a peer (Laurence Olivier) uses the higher style but keeps the knighthood and the entitlement, so the rule as an entitlement has no exception; the well-known members hold no peerage. The Knight Bachelor is the basic knighthood (no order, no post-nominal letters), so 'Sir' comes from it alone for McCartney (1997) and Elton John (1998); later honours (both CH) carry no style. 'Lord': plausible (the style of a peer) and clearly false. Well-known members: their style is stored by name ('Sir Paul McCartney', 'Sir Elton John', each over 90,000 exact-phrase hits), much more often than their knighthood. The prompts ask only the honorific and do not say they were knighted, so w1 does not contradict the prompt. In w1 the member stops being a Knight Bachelor (the tarantula pattern); the side facts that go with it are his own knighting ceremony and year. No fact about another person forces it: a knighthood has no succession or numbering. New members are fictional, named in the prompt as British men in lay professions. Two independent storage choices, four worlds. The near query (the accolade) shares the topic and its answer is not 'Lord'. That one honorific is placed before each well-known member's name is now a bridge with a check on his or her question: 'which honorific' and the clash in the by-name worlds need it (formal check, FINDINGS B3 and C3).
